questions.question: A feature branch carries 9 messy 'wip' commits, and before merging to main the team wants them collapsed into one clean commit with the history rewritten. Which command does the squashing?
questions.explanation: Interactive rebase opens the commit list so commits can be squashed, reordered, edited, or dropped - the standard history-cleanup tool.

questions.question: After 'git push' fails with 'no upstream branch', a colleague runs 'git push -u origin feature-x'; from then on, bare 'git push' and 'git pull' just work on feature-x. What did the -u flag establish?
questions.explanation: The -u/--set-upstream flag links the local branch to a remote-tracking branch so push/pull know their default counterpart.

questions.question: A developer copies a project folder to a USB stick but misses one hidden subdirectory; the copy compiles fine yet has no history, branches, or remotes. Which directory was left behind?
questions.explanation: The .git directory holds the entire object database, refs, config, and metadata - the working tree alone is just the checked-out snapshot.

questions.question: A regression exists in HEAD, but tag v2.0 - 200 commits back - is clean; rather than reading logs, the team marks the good and bad endpoints and lets Git binary-search the culprit. Which command?
questions.explanation: git bisect checks out the midpoint of the suspect range each round; each good/bad verdict halves it, so ~200 commits need only about 8 tests.

questions.question: Branches A and B merged into each other twice in the past, so their next merge has two common ancestors; Git first merges the ancestors into a virtual base, then merges the tips. Which merge strategy does this describe?
questions.explanation: The recursive strategy resolves multiple merge bases by recursively merging them into a temporary virtual ancestor - Git's default approach for complex histories.

questions.question: After 'git checkout 3fa9b2c', Git warns 'You are in detached HEAD state' and .git/HEAD now contains a raw commit hash instead of a branch ref. In this state, what does HEAD point to?
alternatives: the commit itself, not a branch
questions.explanation: Normally HEAD is a symbolic ref to a branch; detached, it points straight at a commit, so new commits belong to no branch.

questions.question: A bad commit is already pushed to the shared main branch, so rewriting history is off the table. Which command undoes its changes via a new inverse commit that leaves history intact?
questions.explanation: git revert creates a new commit applying the inverse diff - safe on shared branches because no existing history is rewritten.

questions.question: Inside .git, branches and tags live as small files holding commit hashes - for example heads/main and tags/v1.0. Under which subdirectory do these pointers sit?
questions.explanation: The refs/ tree stores pointers: refs/heads for branches, refs/tags for tags, refs/remotes for remote-tracking branches.

questions.question: The same file committed in two different repositories yields the identical object ID, because Git names every blob, tree, and commit by a 160-bit hash of its content. Which hash algorithm provides those IDs?
questions.explanation: Git's content-addressable store keys every object by the SHA-1 of its contents, so identical data deduplicates and corruption is detectable.

questions.question: The team wants a script that runs the linter automatically before every local commit, and another that fires on the server when pushes arrive. Under which .git subdirectory do such scripts live?
questions.explanation: The hooks/ directory holds executable scripts Git invokes at lifecycle points - pre-commit locally, pre-receive on the server.

questions.question: After a hard reset deleted commits, which command shows the history of HEAD movements so they can be recovered?
questions.explanation: git reflog records every position HEAD has held, allowing recovery of commits lost after resets or rebases.

questions.question: You forgot to include a file in your last commit. Which flag rewrites that most recent commit to include it?
questions.explanation: git commit --amend replaces the most recent commit, letting you add forgotten changes or fix the message.

questions.question: A shared server repository contains only Git data and no working tree. What is this called?
questions.explanation: A bare repository holds only the .git contents without checked-out files, serving purely as a push/fetch endpoint.

questions.question: A repository must embed another repository's specific commit as a subdirectory. Which Git feature does this?
questions.explanation: Git submodules pin an external repository at a specific commit inside a parent repository's directory tree.

questions.question: A team wants every feature merge to keep a visible merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible. Which flag achieves this?
questions.explanation: The --no-ff flag forces Git to create a merge commit even when fast-forwarding is possible, preserving branch topology.

questions.question: After a bad interactive rebase, 'git reflog' shows the pre-rebase state at HEAD@{3}. The command that returns the branch to that state.
alternatives: git reset --hard HEAD@{3} (or the pre-rebase SHA)
questions.explanation: Reflog entries are valid references; 'git reset --hard HEAD@{3}' moves the branch back to the recorded pre-rebase commit.

questions.question: git bisect: 128 suspect commits lie between a known-good and a buggy commit. The maximum number of test iterations needed to find the culprit.
questions.explanation: Bisect halves the range each step: log2(128) = 7 iterations, worst case, to isolate the bad commit.

questions.question: During release prep, only the 3 middle commits of a 10-commit feature branch must land on main. The command (or equivalent approach) that applies exactly that range.
questions.explanation: 'git cherry-pick A^..B' applies the inclusive commit range onto the current branch; 'rebase --onto' achieves the same for a contiguous series.

questions.question: After 'git commit --amend' on an already-pushed commit, teammates who pulled it hit divergence. Explain why amending published commits breaks shared history.
questions.answer: Amending rewrites history: it creates a new commit object (new SHA), so clones holding the old SHA no longer share ancestry
alternatives: It creates a new SHA - rewritten public history
New commit hash diverges from pulled history
questions.explanation: A commit's identity is its hash; amending produces a different object, so remotes and clones that fetched the original see divergent histories and duplicated changes.

questions.question: In conflict markers '<<<<<<< HEAD ... ======= ... >>>>>>> feature-x', state which branch each section represents.
questions.answer: Between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is the current branch ('ours'); between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming branch 'feature-x' ('theirs')
questions.explanation: The upper block shows the checked-out branch's version (HEAD/ours); the lower block shows the incoming change being merged (theirs).
